title: The third level of Grand Central
body: Charley, hurrying to catch the subway from Grand Central one summer night, follows a corridor that angles left and slopes downward. He hears only his own footsteps until a hollow roar tells him there is open space ahead. Down a short flight of stairs he comes out on a level that at first looks like the second one, but the room is smaller, with fewer ticket windows and train gates. The information booth is wooden and old-looking, and the man in it wears a green eyeshade and black sleeve protectors. The lights flicker because they are open-flame gaslights. There are brass spittoons on the floor; a man in a derby hat and a four-button suit checks a gold watch; a woman wears a dress with leg-of-mutton sleeves; a small locomotive with a funnel-shaped stack stands on the tracks. 'And then I knew,' Charley says. To make sure, he walks to a newsboy and looks at the papers at his feet: it is The World, a paper that has not been published for years, and its lead story is about President Cleveland. He later finds that front page in the Public Library files, printed on June 11, 1894.
